newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Protests greet Philippine oil deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Protests greet Philippine oil deregulation.

text.p: The Philippines freed the oil industry of government price controls on Saturday, sending Filipino drivers to the pumps ahead of deregulation and sparking protest rallies and transport strikes.
"We had a crowd here before the clock struck 12 p.m. (Friday night)," said a salesman at a Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp gas station near Manila's Makati financial district.

By Saturday morning, the queues had disappeared as prices of premium gasoline were raised by an average 41.45 centavos per litre to 11.30 pesos ($0.43). Unleaded prices were raised by an average of 0.66 centavos to 10.8986 pesos per litre.
The government, which had regulated petroleum prices since the 70s, completely freed the industry from Saturday.
Deregulation was greeted with protest rallies by several hundred people and a transport strike in Angeles City near Manila.
Police in Angeles City said commuters were stranded after jeepney (mini-bus) drivers went on strike, crippling 95 percent of public transportation within the city.

Left-wing groups and jeepney drivers also held rallies in Manila and Angeles City to protest against the oil industry deregulation, which they said could lead to price abuses by the country's oil refiners.
Transport and left-wing groups also held a night-long vigil on Friday in front of the offices of oil refiners in the Makati financial centre.
On Saturday, the protesters demonstrated in front of the Presidential Palace and the U.S. embassy.

Shell and the two other major Philippine oil refiners, Petron Corp and Caltex Philippines Inc, have all raised prices for premium gasoline, unleaded gasoline and liquefied petroleum gasoline. But prices of five other petroleum products have been slashed.
Taxi drivers in Manila said they may discard their meters and fix rates "depending on the traffic" to make up for the increase in fuel prices.
"We may have to be more resourceful so that we have extra money to bring home," said taxi driver Morris Sevilla.
Energy Secretary Francisco Viray said prices should stabilise at current levels because of soft international prices.
"Under normal conditions, we expect prices to stabilise at this level, if not drop in the next few months because of the softening of international prices of oil products," he told reporters.
